questions.q: Do we delete the Firebase document-holding design, or adopt it and take the fiduciary and intermediary duty that follows?
questions.lede: Three committed files give three answers, and every legal rule in §22 is a function of this one.

visual.note: Ceiling from the DPDP Schedule; 74 hours itemised at PRD v2 line 4194
visual.caption: What each answer holds, and what duty comes with it

questions.stakes: Adopting it puts document content under a ₹250 crore security ceiling and makes us an intermediary before there is one user.
state: `firestore.rules:318` caps a note body at 900,000 characters, `:361` makes revisions undeletable, and `:393` allows an unauthenticated `get` on any public share.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4295` says we hold user documents. `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:133` says the control plane holds no document bytes.
Nothing writes to Firestore. The rules file calls itself a prototype at `firestore.rules:7` and says harden before taking paid signups.
path: `firestore.rules` landed with the Firebase backend commit and nobody deleted it when the plan moved local-first.
The round-2 sweep found the contradiction on 2026-09-08 (`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:142`) and made it decision 7 (`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:365`).
tension: Holding bytes confers intermediary status under IT Act §2(1)(w), which drags in the 74 founder-hours itemised at `docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4194`.
The one claim a server-side rival cannot copy is that the documents never reach us (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:10104`).
Decision 3's hosted read-only viewer needs a server store, so closing this forecloses it (`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:367`).

options.label: Delete `firestore.rules` and write zero document bytes into §22 as a constraint
options.what: The control plane holds identity, team membership, entitlements and billing, and nothing else.
gains: Legal surface collapses to identity and billing
Keeps the sentence a server-side rival cannot say
Costs no engineering: zero Firestore writes exist
costs: Forecloses hosted publishing, server search and decision 3's viewer
Deletes the only written data model for a server store
options.system: Firestore schema removed; §22 gains a hard architectural constraint.
options.screens: Kills the hosted-viewer screen before it is drawn.
options.money: None today. Forfeits any tier priced on server-side storage.

options.label: Adopt the Firebase design as written
options.what: We store note bodies and an append-only revision history, and serve public reads to anyone.
gains: Hosted sync, server-side search and publishing all become possible
A written data model already exists
costs: Document content falls under §8(5), ceiling ₹250 crore
Intermediary status and 74 founder-hours before the first stranger
options.system: Firestore becomes the store of record and every §22 row is rewritten.
options.screens: Adds a share manager, a revision history and a moderation console.
options.money: Storage and egress at scale, plus counsel for a policy saying we can read documents.

options.label: Hold documents server-side but delete the unauthenticated public-read path
options.what: We keep a server store and drop the anonymous `get` at `firestore.rules:393`.
gains: Intermediary duty mostly falls away
Hosted sync and server search stay available
costs: Fiduciary duty over content stays, with the ₹250 crore ceiling
Still needs processor agreements, an Indian log store and breach cover
options.system: One rule deleted. The store and its duties remain.
options.screens: No share page for strangers; any hosted viewer stays behind sign-in.
options.money: Storage cost plus the processor paperwork in L10.

options.label: Defer past the pilot
options.what: Leave the three files contradicting each other and decide after the ten-stranger test.
gains: Costs nothing this week
costs: §22 cannot be finalised, so no privacy policy can be written
A pilot with no published policy breaches SPDI Rule 4 today

recCase: Nothing writes to Firestore across 226 source files, so deleting the design costs no engineering.
The cost model at 10,000 users and the strongest marketing claim both rest on holding no bytes (`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:133`).
Adoption would be the largest available expansion of legal surface, taken before there is a user to justify it.
questions.flip: If decision 3 lands on a hosted read-only viewer, or a paying team refuses to buy without server-side search, (c) is the honest minimum and the ₹250 crore surface must be budgeted.

questions.q: Do we rewrite the web app to the browser-only byte path before the pilot, or withdraw the zero-bytes claim?
questions.lede: Zero document bytes on our server is the plan's central legal claim, and the shipped code refutes it today.

lines.t: 25 of 26 routes act on the vault server-side
Browser calls api.github.com with the user's token
Server exchanges the App key for a token, nothing else
Client-side index; no server full-text search

visual.note: Routes measured in this repo; the browser path is a draft at WEEK0 line 35
visual.caption: The byte path as shipped, against the path the plan claims

questions.stakes: Leave it as it is and the plan's headline architecture claim is false in the first file a buyer opens.
state: `src/app/api/commit/route.ts:27` accepts 10 MB per file, `src/app/api/ai/refine/route.ts:35` accepts 200,000 characters, and 25 of 26 routes act on the vault server-side.
`docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:35` proposes browser-side only. Nothing implements it, and `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:221` still lists it as open.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:171` cut a vendor CDN for breaking the same rule, while both export renderers still load jsdelivr.
path: 202 of 228 source files are shared with `sgnk-md` (`docs/DECIDE.md:168`), a server-rendered app built against GitHub for one trusted author.
The browser path was drafted on 2026-09-08. `docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:31` says plainly that nobody had written the path down.
tension: `api.github.com` supports CORS, so read and write are known to work in the browser (`docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:33`).
Browser-only forfeits server-side full-text search, which §9 currently assumes (`docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:50`).
On Hobby and trial-Pro plans Vercel may use content to train and share it (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4158`), so on those plans the hosting contract contradicts the claim.

options.label: Rewrite the web app to the browser-only path before the first stranger; keep the claim
options.what: Commit, file read, search and AI move into the page, and the server only mints an installation token.
gains: The claim becomes true and stays the strongest differentiator
Removes the Vercel training clause from the argument entirely
costs: Real work across commit, read, search and AI, plus a GitHub App review
Server-side full-text search is forfeited
options.system: Every vault route is deleted or reduced to a token exchange.
options.screens: Search changes shape; no other screen moves.

options.label: Keep the server path, withdraw the claim, write the real data flow into the policy
options.what: We say plainly that the web app reads and writes documents through our server.
gains: No engineering cost
The policy and the code agree
costs: Loses the sentence a server-side rival cannot say
Pulls in fiduciary duty over content and every obligation in L10
options.money: None now; larger compliance cost later.

options.label: Keep both: server path for the web trial, browser-only on desktop, and say which is which
options.what: The claim is scoped to the desktop app in §1 and §4, and the web trial is disclosed as server-side.
gains: Truthful and cheap
Keeps the zero-install trial
costs: The pilot's ten strangers sit under the larger duty
The marketing line carries an asterisk from day one
options.system: No change to the web app; the desktop build carries the claim.
options.screens: A disclosure on the web trial's first screen.

options.label: Ship the desktop app first and take the web app offline until it is rewritten
options.what: Only the Tauri build is available until the browser path exists.
gains: Removes the contradiction entirely
Focuses the pilot on the daily surface
costs: Costs the zero-install trial, the only friction-free entry point
Adds notarisation and signing to the critical path
options.screens: No web trial screens at all.

recCase: The claim is load-bearing in three places in the plan and under the whole legal design; making it true is cheaper than unwinding what rests on it.
CORS on the GitHub API was verified on 2026-09-08, so the hard part is known to be possible.
It also removes the Vercel training clause from every conversation about where documents go.
questions.flip: If the GitHub App cannot return an installation token to the browser without our server touching the contents API, the open check at `docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:54`, then (c) is the only honest option.

questions.q: Do we treat every legal clock in §22 as already running, or as starting at the pilot?
questions.lede: sgnk-md is the same codebase and is listed as production. If it has users, the clocks started when the first one signed in.

visual.note: GitHub sign-in is allowlisted at auth-options.ts:80; Google sign-in is not

`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:36` records the portfolio listing sgnk-md as production and asks the founders whether there is a user list.

Buys the pilot a clean starting position
costs: About a day of work brought forward
A policy written before L1 and L2 are settled may need rewriting

options.what: We treat the pilot as the first collection of anyone's personal data.
gains: Every §22 deadline stands as written
No work brought forward

Says nothing about Google sign-in, which is not gated

options.what: The sibling deployment stops serving anyone.
gains: Removes any live exposure immediately

Loses the interview pool GAPS:36 names

It needs a founder, not research: is there a user list, and may ten of them be contacted.
If the answer is yes, (b) follows the same week; if no, the pilot is the trigger and nothing is brought forward.

questions.q: Who answers the six-hour clock, and do we file the CERT-In point of contact before there is anything to report?
questions.lede: A six-hour clock with no size floor, one person at 1.21 engineering days a week, and no filed contact.

rows.label: Cost
cells: money and a second credential holder

visual.note: Capacity from PRODUCT-BRIEF line 11; the clock from line 543
visual.caption: Three postures against a clock one person cannot staff

questions.stakes: A reportable incident with no filed contact, no runbook and no logs is the first thing an insurer, an acquirer or an enterprise buyer will find.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:543` states the clock and then records the gap: the Annexure II point-of-contact filing is missing everywhere in our record.
The team is one person: 1.21 engineering days per calendar week and 80 of 80 commits by a single author (`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:11`, `:12`).
No runbook, roster, pager or alert path exists, and `package.json` carries no Sentry, PostHog, Plausible or logging dependency.
path: The CERT-In Directions of 28.04.2022 were read into the record twice (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4122`, `docs/BUSINESS.md:25`) and both passes missed the point-of-contact duty.
An incident runbook was written on 2026-08-29 (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:3697`) and never reached the plan.
The v15 sweep restored the six-hour clock to §22 and did not restore the runbook or ask who runs it.
tension: The clock starts on noticing, so detection gates everything, and there is no detection.
IT Act §70B(7) carries up to one year or ₹1 lakh, though §70B(8) needs a CERT-In officer's complaint first.
The surface that would generate an incident is server-side by construction, which is exactly what L1 and L2 propose to remove.

options.label: File the point of contact now, write the runbook, and state a best-effort clock
options.what: The founder is named, an alert reaches a phone, and the plan says plainly that six hours is best effort.
gains: About a day of work and honest on the face of it
Closes the one gap the record itself flags
costs: A solo founder cannot guarantee six hours
Leaves the whole server-side surface reportable
options.system: Adds alerting to the deploy and a runbook to the repo.

options.label: File now, then shrink the surface until a reportable incident is near impossible
options.what: No server-side documents, no publishing, no hosted AI, so a breach can expose only identity and billing.
gains: Cuts the reportable surface to its smallest set
Costs nothing extra: L1 and L2 already point here
costs: Forecloses the web trial and hosted publishing
Does not remove the duty, only the likely trigger
options.system: Same change as L1(a) and L2(a); no new work.
options.screens: Removes the share and hosted-AI surfaces.

options.label: File now and pay a second responder onto a rota before the pilot
options.what: A contractor or the second founder shares an on-call schedule with production credentials.
gains: Real coverage of a clock we otherwise cannot meet
Answers the first enterprise security questionnaire
costs: Money, and a second holder of production credentials
Expands the access-revocation surface at `docs/BUSINESS.md:767`
options.system: Credential issue and revocation runbook required.
options.money: A retainer before there is revenue.

options.label: File nothing and rely on §70B(8) needing a CERT-In officer's complaint
options.what: We treat the reporting duty as unenforceable at our size and leave the record's gap open.
gains: Costs nothing
costs: Fails the first security questionnaire and any insurer's proposal form
Leaves a named omission in a document a buyer will read

recCase: The only durable answer to a clock you cannot staff is a smaller surface, and L1 and L2 already point at it.
Filing is an hour of work and appears in three of the four options, so the real choice here is the surface, not the form.
Take (a) alongside it: the runbook and the named person are needed whatever the surface, and the filing requires the name anyway.
questions.flip: The first paying team that requires hosted sync makes (c) compulsory, and its cost belongs in the team tier price rather than in the founder's nights.

questions.q: Do we close the shipped publishing surface to founder-only, and adopt noindex and system slugs as a standing rule?
questions.lede: A crawlable public page with user-chosen slugs makes us an intermediary, and none of the apparatus that comes with it exists.

visual.note: Controls from RECORD line 4181; the narrow shape from PRD v2 line 4204
visual.caption: The publishing surface: who reaches it, and what it drags in

questions.stakes: Open it as configured and we take a permanent 24-hour grievance clock, a 36-hour court-order clock and safe-harbour conditions we cannot meet.
state: `src/app/(public)/[slug]/page.tsx:30` sets `robots: { index: true, follow: true }` and `src/app/robots.ts:18` allows crawlers at `/`.
`src/modules/share/domain/slug.ts:4` makes the slug user-chosen, and `src/app/api/share/route.ts:25` gates publishing on sign-in alone with no tier check.
Outbound links get `noopener noreferrer`, not `nofollow ugc` (`src/modules/preview/presentation/markdown/html-policy.ts:214`).
path: The share surface is inherited from sgnk-md and predates the plan's no-hosting rule at `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:43`.
The abuse ranking put SEO spam and backlink farms first and named the controls (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4181`); PRD v2 then recommended exactly that narrow shape at `:4204`.
The plan's own §9 design already sets noindex, nofollow as the default (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:9392`), so the code contradicts the plan as well as the research.
tension: IT Act §79 safe harbour is conditional on the 2021 due-diligence set, and losing it makes the founder a co-defendant on the underlying claim.
74 founder-hours at 1.21 engineering days a week is about seven and a half weeks, and §14's twelve-week plan never schedules it.
Decision 3's hosted read-only viewer is unresolved, and closing publishing pre-empts it (`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:367`).

Buys back roughly seven weeks of apparatus work
costs: Loses whatever distribution a public page brings
Pre-empts decision 3 unless it is revisited

options.screens: The public note page is unreachable for anyone else.

gains: Keeps the feature and cuts the abuse surface sharply
Produces the artefacts a B2B buyer asks for
costs: 74 founder-hours does not fit before week 1 of the pilot
The 24-hour clock then runs every day, permanently
options.system: Adds a report form, a ticket store, a preservation store and an action log.
options.screens: Adds a report page, a grievance page and a moderation console.
options.money: Seven and a half weeks of founder time at the measured rate.

options.what: Any signed-in user publishes a root-level, crawlable page under a slug they choose.
gains: Keeps the organic channel argument alive
costs: Ships the shape the abuse research ranked first, with no takedown apparatus
Cloudflare terminates accounts for user-chosen deceptive names
options.system: No change, which is the problem.

One less surface for L16's review to cover

Throws away code that mostly works

recCase: Publishing is not on the MVP-0 critical path; §14's twelve-week plan never schedules it.
It is the single feature that turns a tool into an intermediary with a permanent 24-hour clock.
The standing rule costs nothing to hold while publishing is closed and binds automatically the day it opens, so it is worth setting once.
The plan already refuses a footer backlink for the same reason (`docs/BUSINESS.md:1046`), so indexable user pages would contradict settled reasoning.
questions.flip: If decision 3 lands on the hosted viewer as the thing Pro sells, (b) is the shape, the 74 hours enter the schedule ahead of the pilot, and the tier price has to carry them.

questions.q: Do we publish a privacy policy, terms and a named grievance officer before the pilot, and which redressal window do they promise?
questions.lede: SPDI Rule 4 requires a published policy today, the app has four pages, and none of them is a policy.

visual.title: Pages served on the live app
visual.note: privacy and terms are reserved slugs with no route behind them; grievance is not reserved
visual.caption: Four pages exist; the three the live regime requires do not

questions.stakes: The pilot puts ten strangers into an app that takes an email at first run with no notice, no consent step and no page to point at.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:542` lists as due now: a published privacy policy, consent before collection, a named grievance officer within one month, and a transfer gate.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:548` adds the ninety-day ceiling from 2027-05-13 and notes §13(3) makes our channel the mandatory first stop before the Board.
No person is named anywhere in the corpus, and `privacy` and `terms` are reserved slugs with no route behind them (`src/modules/share/domain/slug.ts:43`).
path: The v15 sweep corrected a register that had assumed DPDP was operative, which moved the policy duty from 2027 to today.

A published window is a promise, and missing your own published window is worse than publishing a modest one.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:536` says email is collected only when an obligation exists and never at first run, which the sign-in screen already contradicts.

options.label: Publish all three before the pilot, self-drafted, one month, founder named

gains: The pilot runs lawfully and costs less than one week of measured capacity
The window matches the live regime exactly
costs: A self-drafted policy may say something we later correct
The page needs revisiting the day L6 changes
options.system: Three static routes plus a monitored address.
options.screens: Adds /privacy, /terms and /grievance, linked from the footer and from sign-in.
options.money: Founder time now; counsel's fee deferred.

options.label: Counsel drafts them first, then the pilot
options.what: An Indian firm writes the three documents before any stranger sees the app.
gains: A reviewed document from the start
One review covers the CERT-In filing and the terms together
costs: Spends ₹40,000–1,20,000 before any evidence anyone wants the product
Delays the pilot by whatever the review takes

options.label: A written notice by hand to each of the ten, full pages at MVP-1
options.what: Each pilot participant gets a one-page notice; nothing is published on the site.
gains: Proportionate to ten known participants and cheap
costs: Does not satisfy the published-policy duty while anyone else can reach the app
Today anyone can reach the app

options.label: Publish the tightest window from day one: 24-hour ack, 15-day resolution
options.what: We promise the intermediary-grade window whether or not publishing is open.
gains: Simplest to explain and never wrong
No revisiting when L6 changes
costs: Binds one person to a daily acknowledgement duty before anything requires it
A missed self-imposed window is worse than a modest one
options.system: Needs a monitored inbox with a same-day rota.
options.money: None in cash; real in attention.

recCase: Twelve hours of writing is less than one week of measured capacity and it removes a live breach.
Publish the window that binds and no tighter, because a published window is a promise we then have to keep.
The honest version is short, because the architecture genuinely holds very little.
§13(3) later turns this channel into a shield, so it is worth building properly rather than minimally.

questions.q: Do we geo-exclude the EU for the pilot, or accept EU users and budget an Art 27 representative?
questions.lede: GDPR Art 3(2)(a) catches a free tool, and §22 concedes the targeting posture addresses that limb only.

rows.label: Who spots the first EU seat

questions.q: Does the review sidecar carry a person's real identity into the user's git repository, or a pseudonymous id?
questions.lede: The one file the product exists to write is the one place nobody asked what personal data it carries.

visual.name: .frontmatter/review.jsonl
visual.note: Fields from PRODUCT-BRIEF line 135; the file is committed beside the documents
visual.caption: The one file the product writes, and what of it is personal data

questions.stakes: An erasure request against a sidecar in a repository we do not control has no answer, because git cannot forget without rewriting history.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:135` specifies the sidecar as one JSON line per span carrying reviewed-by, reviewed-at and, when known, author, model and prompt.
It is committed alongside the documents, and the web byte path writes it by the same path as the documents (`docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:43`).
`reviewed-by` appears once in the whole plan and never in any legal section.
path: The sidecar was designed as an engineering artefact: a durable anchor that survives other tools writing to the file.
The legal sweep on 2026-09-08 covered breach, retention, residency, transfer, grievance and the EU, and never looked at the product's own output file.
tension: If the repository is public, the identity and every review timestamp are published; if private, they are shared with everyone who can clone.
DPDP §12(3) and GDPR Art 17 both give erasure on request, and we control none of it (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:8888`).
The prompt field is the user's own instruction text and may contain anything they would not knowingly commit.

options.label: Store a per-repo pseudonymous id by default, with a local map the user owns
options.what: The file carries a stable id; the interface resolves it to a name only on the reader's own machine.
gains: Removes the identifier from the artefact that leaves our control
Cross-tool review state still works: the id is stable within the repo
costs: A team buyer wanting human-readable names in the file does not get them
Needs a local map and a rule for what happens when it is missing
options.system: Adds an id-to-name map outside the repo and an id minting rule.
options.screens: The review panel shows names; the file shows ids.

options.label: Store real identity and say so plainly in the docs and at first write
options.what: The sidecar carries an email or handle, and the product warns the first time a line is written.
gains: Most legible to a team that wants to know who read what
No mapping layer to build or lose
costs: Publishes a person's reading history into a repo forever, with no erasure route
Makes every rights request unanswerable
options.screens: A first-write notice, prominent rather than buried in a policy.

options.label: Keep the sidecar out of the repo, machine-local and synced separately
options.what: Review state never travels with the documents.
gains: Removes the exposure entirely
costs: Destroys the central claim: review state across people and tools needs the file to travel
Turns a plain-text artefact into a sync problem
options.system: A separate store and a sync path, which the plan says it does not want.
options.money: Sync infrastructure the plan defers to MVP-2.

options.label: Drop the prompt field, keep identity, document the rest
options.what: The highest-variance field goes; the identity and timestamp trail stays.
gains: Removes the field most likely to carry something private
One-line change
costs: Leaves the identity and timestamp trail intact and unerasable
Loses the prompt evidence that makes attribution useful
options.system: One field removed from the writer.
options.screens: The panel no longer shows what was asked.

recCase: The product needs a stable per-span identity, not a person's name, so a pseudonymous id costs nothing functionally.
It removes the only irreversible personal-data flow the architecture creates.
Take (d) at the same time: the prompt field is the one most likely to carry something a user would never knowingly commit.
questions.flip: If the team feature turns out to need human-readable attribution in the file for the buyer to trust it, then (b) with a prominent notice at the first sidecar write, never buried in a policy.

questions.q: Do we build the India-resident 180-day log store now, or run with no logs at all and say so?
questions.lede: The plan says the log residency is already priced, and the store it was priced against is not the stack we run.

lines.t: 180 days rolling, NTP to NIC or NPL
no bytes, no filenames, no cleartext IP
Vercel and Firebase, no region pinned
zero logs, so nothing to capture

visual.note: The R2 design is at PRD v2 line 3689; the residency conflict was recorded at RECORD line 4122
visual.caption: The log store was priced on infrastructure the product does not use

questions.stakes: A breach investigation with no log slice is an investigation with no evidence, and the 180 days is a floor rather than a ceiling.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:544` states 180 days of ICT logs inside Indian jurisdiction and says it is already priced as R2 with object-lock.
The running stack is Vercel plus Firebase with no region pinned, and `package.json` carries no logging, error-reporting or analytics dependency.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:3689` specifies the content: NTP-synced timestamp, request id, opaque user id, action verb, and no document bytes.
path: The residency duty was read from the CERT-In Directions on 2026-08-29 and `docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4122` recorded the conflict with a default Cloudflare stack at the time.
The stack then changed to Vercel and Firebase and the pricing line did not.
tension: The real position is not a residency problem but an absence: there are no logs at all.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:545` states the 180 days as a floor, and adds a one-year access-log floor from 2027-05-13.
If L1 and L2 close the server surface, the log volume approaches zero and the store becomes almost empty by construction.

options.label: Build the minimal India-resident append-only security log now
options.what: Timestamp, request id, opaque user id, verb and outcome, and nothing else.
gains: Satisfies the floor and gives a breach response something to capture
Five opaque fields hold no content and little personal data
costs: Adds one vendor and one region decision to a one-person stack
Needs NTP sync and an object-lock equivalent
options.system: A write-only store and a request-id middleware.
options.money: Small storage cost; one more vendor to paper under L10.

options.label: Run with no logs through the pilot and state that plainly in the runbook
options.what: We hold nothing, and the plan says so rather than implying a store exists.
gains: Zero cost and zero personal data at rest
costs: Leaves the 180-day floor unmet and any incident un-investigable
The first security questionnaire finds it

options.label: Turn on the host's own logs and accept whatever region they land in
options.what: Platform logging is enabled with default settings.
gains: Cheapest way to have logs at all
costs: Fails the residency clause
Default settings capture paths and IPs, which PRD v2 line 3689 forbids in this store
options.system: A configuration change, no new code.

options.label: Correct §22 to name the real stack and defer the store to MVP-1
options.what: The plan stops citing an R2 price for a Vercel and Firebase deployment.
gains: Honest and free
Stops a wrong price being quoted as if it applied
costs: Keeps the gap open
Fixes the document, not the duty

recCase: The store is five opaque fields, append-only, with no content, and it is the one artefact a breach response cannot reconstruct afterwards.
Do (d) regardless of the answer: the priced design is R2 on Cloudflare and the running stack is not.
It also gives L4's runbook something to point at when the six-hour clock starts.
questions.flip: If L1 and L2 close the server-side surface completely, the log volume approaches zero and (b) with a written statement becomes defensible for the pilot only.

questions.q: Do we pay for a trademark knock-out search now, rename before launch, or ship qualified and accept the exposure?
questions.lede: An 82,265-install incumbent owns the word in the exact store the product might ship to, and no clearance search has been run.

items.label: Knock-out search, or rename
items.note: at zero users the rename is free

visual.note: Dates from GAPS line 132 and PRD v2 line 4829
visual.caption: The name got worse in the ten days nobody was watching it

questions.stakes: A rebrand after the domain, the logo and the launch copy are paid for costs many times what it costs today at zero users.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:13` records 82,265 installs of the extension that already owns the name.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4845` says plainly that nothing done so far is a clearance: USPTO, EUIPO, IP India and WIPO are all unchecked.
`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:132` adds that Frontmatter Studio was taken on 2026-09-07 and the `@frontmatter` npm scope is the incumbent's.
path: The collision was in the record on 2026-08-29 at 80,605 installs and the plan never mentioned it until the round-2 sweep (`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:50`).
`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:150` now lists the name as a legal question and not only a marketing one.
tension: A EU word mark for FRONTMATTER is reported but was never reproduced from five blocked registries (`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:146`), so the deciding fact is unverified.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4841` names the falsifier as an attorney's knock-out search on the incumbent's class overlap.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4839` rates the halfway version, the bare word plus quiet qualified handles, as the highest-risk option.

options.label: Commission an attorney's knock-out search on the final two candidates before any spend
options.what: A professional clears, or does not clear, the name in the overlapping class.
gains: The step the plan's own falsifier prescribes
Turns an unverified report into a decision
costs: A fee and a short wait
Two candidate names have to be chosen first
options.money: One attorney's fee, before the domain and logo spend.

options.label: Rename now to a clean coinage and stop paying attention to it
options.what: We pick a name nobody else holds and move on.
gains: Removes the risk and the permanent "not the VS Code one" tax
At zero users the rename is close to free
costs: Throws away whatever recognition the name has, which is little
A coinage has to be found and cleared too
options.system: Repo, package and Tauri identity all change.
options.money: A new domain; the old spend is small.

options.label: Keep the name but qualify it, and keep the bare word off the store listing
options.what: The spoken name is qualified everywhere, not only in the handles.
gains: Keeps continuity with the record and the repo
costs: A half-qualified name is rated the highest-risk option with extra steps
Search and word of mouth still collide with 82,265 installs
options.system: Naming rule across the app and the store listing.

options.label: Ship bare and deal with it if a letter arrives
options.what: We use the bare word in the incumbent's own store and wait.
gains: Costs nothing today
costs: Maximum exposure in an overlapping class with a near-identical mark
Any rebrand then happens after the launch spend
options.money: Nothing now; a full rebrand later.

recCase: Everything else about the name is preference; whether a registered mark exists in an overlapping class is the only input that changes the answer.
It has never been checked, and every registry the record tried was blocked.
The spend it gates, domain, logo, launch copy and store listing, is all still ahead of us.
questions.flip: A clean knock-out makes a qualified name viable and (c) right; a hit in the incumbent's class makes (b) the only option, and sooner is cheaper because at zero users the rename is free.

questions.q: Do we buy an outside security review before the first non-founder user, and does it cover the shipped code or only the Firestore design?
questions.lede: We assert our own safety, and the shipped code carries a defect two files revealed in one reading pass.

visual.note: Binding at next.config.ts:48; the report-only policy at proxy.ts:112 and :117
visual.caption: The defect two files revealed, with no outside review bought

questions.stakes: The people who wrote the code are judging whether it is safe, and the first B2B buyer will ask for the artefact we do not have.
state: `docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:44` lists an outside security review as untapped, with the trigger set at before the first team customer.
`firestore.rules:7` labels itself a prototype and says harden before taking paid signups, and `docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:146` gives the review a concrete subject.
`next.config.ts:48` binds the enforced CSP to `/p/:slug*`, which is now only a redirect, so the live public page falls back to the report-only policy at `src/proxy.ts:112`.
path: The rules file carried its own warning from the commit that introduced it, and nobody acted on it.
The v15 sweep gave the review a subject and did not schedule or scope it.
The written trigger, before the first team customer, is later than the pilot, so ten strangers would use the product first.
tension: `src/proxy.ts:117` permits `unsafe-eval` in the policy that actually applies to untrusted content.
The comments in both files still describe the old arrangement as if it holds, which is how the defect survived.
If L1 and L2 both close the server surface, the thing to review shrinks to almost nothing.

options.label: Buy a scoped external review of the shipped code and the Firestore design before the pilot
options.what: An outside reviewer covers the routes, the CSP, the auth paths and the rules file.
gains: Finds the class of defect above, which two files revealed in one pass
Produces the artefact the first B2B buyer asks for
costs: A fee and about a week, before there is any revenue
Reviews a server surface L1 and L2 may be about to delete

options.label: Fix the known defects internally and defer the review to the first team customer
options.what: We repair the CSP binding ourselves and keep the trigger as written.
gains: Free now
costs: Keeps the pattern that produced the defect
Ten strangers use the product before anyone outside has looked

options.label: Review only `firestore.rules`, the named concrete subject
options.what: The scope is the design document and nothing that executes.
gains: Cheapest scoping
costs: Reviews a file nothing runs while the code that does run goes unreviewed
Pointless if L1 deletes the file
options.money: A small fee for little coverage.

options.label: Take L1 and L2 first, then buy a scoped review of a much smaller product
options.what: Delete the Firestore design and close the server surface, then review what is left.
gains: The cheapest real review is the one with the smallest subject
Aligns the spend with the architecture we intend to ship
costs: Pushes the review past the pilot
Depends on two other decisions going the same way
options.system: Follows L1(a) and L2(a); no new work here.

recCase: The cheapest security review is the one with the smallest subject, and L1 and L2 already point at a product with almost no server.
Take those first and this becomes a modest scoped review rather than an audit of a document platform.
Fix the CSP binding this week regardless: it is two lines, and untrusted content is currently served under a policy that reports rather than enforces.
questions.flip: If L1 goes to (b) or (c) and we hold documents server-side, the review moves ahead of the pilot and (a) stops being optional.

questions.q: What does the privacy policy promise about deletion, given that retention now has a floor as well as a ceiling?
questions.lede: We cannot promise to delete what the law requires us to keep, and the record still carries the rule the v15 sweep says to delete.

items.label: Access logs plus the data they concern, 1 year

visual.note: Floors from PRODUCT-BRIEF line 545; the superseded ceiling from RECORD line 4508
visual.caption: Every retention rule that binds today is a floor, not a ceiling

questions.stakes: A policy saying we delete what you delete is false the day it is published, and the user finds out at the moment it matters most.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:545` sets the floors and instructs that the record's no-row-level-retention-beyond-90-days rule be deleted.
That rule is still in the record at `docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4508`, so someone will quote it.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:546` separately kills the inactivity-erasure timer: the Third Schedule thresholds do not reach us.
path: The 90-day rule was written on 2026-08-29 from DPDP §8(7)(a) as a ceiling.
The v15 sweep read the notified Rules and found floors the earlier pass had not seen.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4123` already advised naming the conflict in the policy rather than letting a user discover it, and no policy exists to carry the advice.
tension: The floors that bind today are CERT-In's and the IT Rules', not DPDP's, so the schedule cannot wait for 2027.
A statutory books-of-account floor also applies and its period is unverified (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:3064`).
If L1, L2 and L14 all close the server surface, most of the table disappears and the honest claim gets shorter.

options.label: Publish a retention table naming the floors and what survives an account closure
options.what: The policy carries a row per record type, its period, and the rule that sets it.
gains: Doubles as the internal schedule, so it is written once and used twice
It is the artefact a rights request is answered from
costs: A longer policy than the convention
Every row has to be true, which means checking the Companies Act floor
options.system: Forces a written record inventory before the page can be published.
options.money: Founder time; possibly one CA question.

options.label: Promise deletion on request with an except-where-law-requires clause
options.what: The conventional short form, with the exceptions unnamed.
gains: Short and conventional
Fast to write
costs: The user discovers the exceptions when they matter, which RECORD:4123 advised against
Gives a rights request nothing to answer from

options.label: Hold nothing that needs retaining, so the retention schedule is genuinely near-empty
options.what: Deletion is trivial because there is almost nothing outside identity and billing.
gains: The shortest honest policy available
The architecture does the work instead of the wording
costs: Only reachable if L1, L2 and L14 all close the server surface
CERT-In's floor and the billing records still apply
options.system: Follows L1, L2 and L14; no new work here.

options.label: Defer the retention schedule until DPDP commences
options.what: We treat retention as a 2027 problem.
gains: No work now
costs: Wrong direction: the binding floors today are CERT-In's and the IT Rules'
Leaves a superseded rule live in a governing document

recCase: A retention table is the single most useful page a privacy policy carries and it doubles as the internal schedule.
Delete the superseded 90-day rule from the record in the same edit; a refuted rule left in a governing document is how a wrong number gets quoted six months later.
The floors are already written down, so the table is transcription rather than research.
questions.flip: If (c) becomes true after L1, L2 and L14, the table gets much shorter and the honest claim gets stronger, not weaker.

questions.q: Do we ship the local hand-collected usage file, a rotating install id, or an account-keyed opt-in upload?
questions.lede: The plan's own EU row calls a persistent rotating install id the fact pattern that triggers Art 3(2)(b) monitoring.

rows.label: What leaves the machine
cells: nothing until a person sends it
a daily count line, on consent

rows.label: Signal after the pilot
cells: only from those who opt in

rows.label: Build cost
cells: a salt store and a rotation timer

visual.note: Designs from WEEK0 lines 19 and 24, and RECORD line 4513
visual.caption: Three measurement designs, and the legal basis each one needs

questions.stakes: The MVP-0 exit gate, six of ten strangers, is unobservable under this architecture unless the measure is designed before week 10.
state: `docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:19` proposes `.frontmatter/usage.jsonl` in the user's repo: counts only, no content, no file names.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:550` warns that a persistent rotating install ID is the Recital 24 monitoring fact pattern, and `:538` says usage counts stay in a local sidecar.
`package.json` carries no PostHog, Plausible, Sentry or analytics dependency, so this is an open choice rather than a migration.
path: The measurement problem was raised because the architecture makes churn unobservable; Obsidian, with the same architecture, states it cannot see churn (`docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:13`).
The rotating-id design came earlier from `docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4513`, which recorded the ePrivacy strict-necessity question as contested and unresolved.
tension: The two designs sit in the same plan and are not the same design: one collects nothing, the other stores an identifier on the user's device.
India has no legitimate-interests limb, so any keyed telemetry needs §4(1)(a) consent (`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4515`).
The fallback at `docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:27` makes the gate self-reported, which is weak evidence for a decision that kills or funds the product.

options.label: Ship the local file as drafted; ask each of the ten to paste it once
options.what: Counts live in the user's own repo and reach us only if a person sends them.
gains: Zero processing by us and no identifier on anyone's device
Fits the architecture's own claims exactly
costs: Ten data points, collected by hand
No signal at all after the pilot
options.system: A daily line writer in the sidecar directory.
options.screens: A settings row saying where the file lives.

options.label: Add a rotating install id with a first-run toggle
options.what: A salted identifier regenerated every 90 days gives a continuous signal.
gains: A continuous measure that survives the pilot
costs: Puts an identifier on terminal equipment on a basis the record calls contested
Matches the Art 3(2)(b) pattern §22 flags
options.system: A salt store, a rotation timer and an upload path.
options.screens: A first-run toggle, which the plan says not to put before value.

options.label: Account-keyed opt-in upload of the same daily line, off by default
options.what: The same counts, tied to an account, sent only on explicit consent.
gains: A clean legal basis and a continuous signal for those who opt in
Works because sign-in is already the first screen
costs: Personal data once keyed, so it carries notice and consent duties
Opt-in rates are unknown at this size
options.system: An endpoint, a consent record and a settings toggle.
options.screens: A settings toggle, off by default.

options.label: Measure nothing and ask the ten a question on day 14
options.what: The gate becomes self-reported by message.
gains: Cheapest, and already drafted as the fallback
costs: Self-reported evidence for a decision that kills or funds the product
No record of what anyone actually did

recCase: For a ten-person pilot the local file is enough, and it is the only option that does not weaken a claim the whole product rests on.
It keeps L12 simple: with no identifier and no upload, the Art 3(2)(b) argument has nothing to attach to.
The file is the user's, in their repo, which is the same rule as the sidecar.
questions.flip: At scale the hand-collection stops working, and (c) is then the right design, consent-based and off by default, rather than (b) on a basis the record calls unresolved.

One fee

options.label: Treat it as immaterial at current spend and revisit at revenue
options.what: We accept the position and carry on.
gains: Cheapest today
costs: Interest and penalty accrue on whatever is owed
Found later, by someone else, during diligence

recCase: This is a factual question about our own filings that nobody in the record has answered, and it should not be guessed from a plan document.
One consultation settles it along with the export-of-services and LUT positions marked unverified at `docs/BUSINESS.md:698`.
The cost of asking is one fee; the cost of being wrong compounds quietly.
questions.flip: If the CA confirms registration is already due, (a) follows immediately, and (c) becomes an attractive way to shrink the exposure while the paperwork catches up.

questions.q: Do we split the licence, Apache-2.0 for the engine and proprietary for the app, or license the repository one way?
questions.lede: The repo states no licence at all, so the default is all rights reserved and nobody may lawfully run the engine.

visual.note: Repo today: no LICENSE, no license field, 47 MIT runtime dependencies
visual.caption: The split the plan reasoned twice and never wrote to disk

questions.stakes: A certificate strategy whose value rises with third-party verification currently forbids third parties from running the engine at all.
state: There is no `LICENSE` or `NOTICE` file, and `package.json` has no `license` field; it declares `private: true`.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4636` records the same measurement and calls all rights reserved the worst position for a spec others should implement.
The proposed split is set out at `:4640`, `:4641` and `:4645`, and again at `docs/ENGINE.md:2237`.
path: The licence was reasoned on 2026-08-29 around the certificate: Apache-2.0 §6 withholds trademark rights, so a fork could not issue certificates in our name.
FSL and BUSL were rejected because the Competing Use clause bars the independent reimplementation that would prove the engine correct.
tension: The repo shares 202 of 228 files with `sgnk-md` (`docs/DECIDE.md:168`), and nobody has checked what the sibling declares.
A root licence will not cover the spec prose, so per-path declarations are needed.
The split describes a boundary the code does not yet have, because the engine is not a separate package.

options.label: Apache-2.0 with NOTICE for the engine, proprietary for the app, per-directory files
options.what: The split already reasoned is written to disk, with a LICENSE in each directory it governs.
gains: Matches reasoning written twice already
The trademark reservation is the mechanism the certificate needs
costs: Requires actually separating the engine into its own package
Per-path declarations to keep in step as the tree moves
options.system: Engine extraction, root and per-directory LICENSE files, a license field.

options.label: One proprietary licence for the whole repository
options.what: Everything is closed and nobody outside may run any of it.
gains: Simplest, and true to the current code layout
costs: Forecloses the third-party verification the certificate strategy depends on
Contradicts publishing a spec for others to implement
options.system: One root LICENSE and a license field.

options.label: Apache-2.0 for everything
options.what: The editor and the engine are both open.
gains: Maximum adoption and the easiest verification story
costs: Hands the whole editor to anyone, including the incumbent we may be colliding with
Nothing left to sell but the service

options.label: Leave it unlicensed until the engine is extracted
options.what: The status quo, which is all rights reserved by default.
gains: No work now
costs: Every day nobody may lawfully verify the engine
The worst position for a spec we intend others to implement

recCase: The reasoning is done and written down twice; what is missing is the file.
Apache-2.0's trademark reservation is the specific mechanism that lets the engine be verified without letting a fork issue certificates in our name.
Check what the sibling repo declares in the same pass, because 202 files are shared.
questions.flip: If the engine will not be extracted as a package in the next quarter, (b) plus a written intent to open it later is more honest than a licence describing a boundary the code does not have.

questions.q: Do we adopt the rule that an unverifiable citation is dropped rather than repeated, and apply it to the gazette number now?
questions.lede: Four governing documents cite one instrument four ways, and every legal deadline in the plan derives from it.

nodes.label: Every deadline in §22
nodes.note: all of them derive from this date

visual.note: The instruction to open the Gazette or drop the number is at PRD v2 line 5982
visual.caption: One unopened source, four citations, every legal deadline downstream

questions.stakes: A visible inconsistency in the documents shown to counsel, sitting on top of the date that fixes every deadline in §22.
state: `docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:541` cites G.S.R. 843(E) of 13 Nov 2025; `docs/BUSINESS.md:26` and `docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:8357` cite 846(E) of the same date.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:4516` cites 846(E) and dates the notification 14 November 2025, deriving a commencement one day later.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-PRD-v2-2026-08-29.md:5982` already recorded the instruction: open the Gazette or drop the number.
path: The number entered the record on 2026-08-29 from a PIB release, marked unverified because the primary registries were unreachable.
The instruction was not followed, and the v15 sweep then introduced a third variant.
tension: `docs/DECIDE.md:212` records that 62% of load-bearing claims needed correction once someone opened a primary source, so there are many more of these.
13 versus 14 November shifts the whole eighteen-month tranche by a day, and the 247-day headline with it.
A marker only works if it travels with the number, and three of four documents dropped it while copying.

options.label: Adopt the rule and apply it now: one attempt at the Gazette, then one number or none
options.what: Unverifiable detail is dropped rather than repeated, starting with the gazette number.
gains: Fixes the date every legal rule derives from
Gives every future citation a default and removes a visible inconsistency
costs: Loses the lead for anyone who later wants to verify it
About an hour, plus edits in four documents
options.system: A citation rule in the docs conventions.

options.label: Adopt the rule but keep unverified details behind an explicit marker
options.what: The number stays with an [SS] tag that must travel with every copy.
gains: Preserves the lead for a later verification pass
costs: The marker is only as good as the reader's attention
Three of four documents already dropped it while copying
options.system: A marker convention and a check for it.

options.label: Standardise on 846(E) because three documents use it
options.what: The inconsistency is resolved by majority.
gains: Fastest to apply
costs: Resolves by majority rather than by source
That is exactly how a wrong number becomes a settled one

options.label: No rule; treat each citation on its merits
options.what: The status quo.
gains: No process to maintain
costs: The status quo produced four citations of one instrument
And a 62% correction rate on load-bearing claims

recCase: The rule is worth more than the number, because it generalises to every other unverified claim in the corpus.
The correction rate says there are many, and the gazette number is the test case.
It also settles whether the 247-day headline in §22 is right.
questions.flip: If the founders want unverified leads preserved for a later verification pass, (b) is defensible, but only with a rule that the marker travels with the number, which is exactly what failed here.

questions.q: Do we state 18-plus in the terms, build an age gate, or write down why the question is out of scope?
questions.lede: DPDP §9 carries a ₹200 crore ceiling, the plan never mentions children, and the code has no age field.

rows.label: Cost
cells: a field, a check and friction

visual.note: Ceiling from RECORD line 4517; the prohibition from RECORD line 4507
visual.caption: Three positions on an obligation the plan never mentions

questions.stakes: The current position is silence, which is the only one of the three that cannot be explained to anyone who asks.
state: `docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4507` quotes §9(3): no tracking or behavioural monitoring of children, and no targeted advertising directed at them.
`docs/FRONTMATTER-RECORD.md:4517` gives the ceiling: ₹200 crore for the §9 children obligations.
There is no age field, no date of birth and no terms acceptance anywhere in `src/`, and §22 does not mention children.
path: The children provisions were captured on 2026-08-29 as a never-collect line inside the telemetry section and never revisited.
The v15 legal sweep covered breach, retention, residency, transfer, grievance and the EU, and did not cover §9.
tension: A markdown editor for repositories has a small realistic child population, but small is an assumption nobody has written down.
The obligation does not scale with the number of children affected.
§9 commences 2027-05-13 with §§3–17 (`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:541`), so the clause is cheap now and awkward later.

options.label: State 18-plus in the terms and do no behavioural monitoring of anyone
options.what: One clause in the terms, alongside the no-monitoring rule the plan already holds.
gains: Costs one sentence and makes §9(3) trivially satisfied
Pairs with L18's no-telemetry answer at no extra cost
costs: A clause nobody reads is weak evidence of anything
Needs the terms page from L7 to exist first

options.label: Build verifiable age assurance at sign-up
options.what: A date-of-birth field and a check before the first screen.
gains: The strongest position if the audience assumption is ever wrong
costs: Real friction on the first screen, which the plan names as the worst place for it
Disproportionate to a developer-tool audience
options.system: An age field, storage and a verification path.
options.screens: Adds a step before the editor.
options.money: A verification vendor if assurance is real rather than self-declared.

options.label: Write down that the product is not directed at children, and publish nothing
options.what: The reasoning goes into §22 and no clause appears in the terms.
gains: Documents the position internally at no cost
costs: Publishes nothing, so the argument is not available to anyone who asks
The gap in the legal section stays visible

options.label: Leave it unaddressed until DPDP commences
options.what: The question waits until 2027-05-13.
gains: No work now
costs: Defers a clause that costs one sentence
Leaves a visible hole at a ₹200 crore penalty tier

recCase: A terms clause costs one sentence and the substantive prohibition is already satisfied by an architecture that monitors nobody.
The reasoning belongs in §22 alongside the other legal rows rather than staying in the record.
It is the only position of the three that can be explained to a buyer or a regulator on sight.
questions.flip: If the product ever ships a public publishing surface aimed at note-takers rather than developers, the audience assumption changes and (b) has to be re-argued on evidence.

questions.q: Do we cite regulators at all, and do we say plainly that none of them requires per-span review?
questions.lede: Nothing opened in the 2026-09-09 research round mandates review below the whole document, and a compliance buyer will check.

rows.label: 21 CFR 11.10(e)
cells: changes must not obscure previously recorded information

rows.label: MHRA GxP data integrity
cells: audit trails may be reviewed by exception reporting

rows.label: EMA reflection paper, 2024
cells: model-generated text needs a quality review mechanism
non-binding, says should, names no granularity

visual.note: All five opened in the 2026-09-09 round; none mandates per-span review
visual.caption: What regulators require, against what a pitch might imply

questions.stakes: One implied mandate that a compliance buyer can refute kills the credibility of every other claim in the deck.
state: The 2026-09-09 round opened 21 CFR 11.10(e), the MHRA GxP data integrity guide and the EMA reflection paper of 9 September 2024.
None mandates per-span review; pharma requires whole-document approval and aviation a per-page revision date.
`docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:541` already carries the discipline for the adjacent case: claim neither compliance nor exposure before the dates.
path: Regulated-document buyers were reached for through desk research; nobody has asked one what an audit trail must contain (`docs/GAPS-2026-09-08.md:41`).
The same round found that a third of the researchers' quotation marks were paraphrases, so every regulator quote needs re-fetching before it is used.
tension: MHRA already permits exception reporting rather than a full list, which supports the product's design and undercuts an enumerate-everything pitch.
The EMA paper says should, is non-binding, and names no granularity, so quoting it as a requirement is the exact overreach a buyer will catch.
Saying plainly that nothing mandates per-span review is a weaker sentence and a stronger position.

options.label: Cite regulators only with the caveat that none mandates per-span review
options.what: Every regulator reference carries the limit of what it actually requires, in the same sentence.
gains: Compliance buyers reward the caveat and punish its absence
Keeps MHRA's exception-reporting line, which supports the design
costs: A longer, flatter sentence than a mandate claim
Every quote must be re-fetched and string-matched first
options.screens: Wording on the regulated-buyer page, if one exists.

options.label: Do not cite regulators at all; sell on the working-tree case alone
options.what: No regulatory language appears anywhere in the pitch.
gains: Nothing to refute and nothing to re-fetch
costs: Gives up the one adjacency where document review is already a habit
MHRA's exception-reporting support goes unused

options.label: Cite them as pressure without the caveat
options.what: Regulators are named to imply a requirement we do not spell out.
gains: The strongest-sounding version
costs: A compliance buyer refutes it from the source in one reading
One refuted claim discredits the rest of the deck

options.label: Defer until five regulated-document buyers have been asked what they need
options.what: The claim waits for the conversations the plan already schedules.
gains: Evidence before wording, which is the right order
costs: Leaves the pitch without a regulated story in the meantime
The conversations have not started

recCase: The caveat costs a clause and it is the sentence a compliance buyer is testing for.
MHRA's exception-reporting line already argues for the product's design, so the honest citation is also the useful one.
Re-fetch and string-match before any regulator quote reaches a slide; roughly one in three of the researchers' quotation marks was a paraphrase.
questions.flip: If the five regulated-buyer conversations turn up a written internal requirement for span-level review, the claim changes from none-mandates to buyers-require, which is a stronger and different sentence.
